cover.artAlt: Enormous golden sand dunes at sunset, with rippled sand stretching to the horizon under a warm orange sky
cover.blurb: Beyond these golden dunes at sunset, the desert is bursting with surprises. Turn the page to meet the plants and animals that make this sandy world their home.

pages.title: The Cactus That Blooms at Night
pages.artAlt: A tall saguaro cactus in bloom stands in front of red rock mesas

facts.text: The saguaro's large flowers are creamy white and open at night. They give off a strong, sweet scent that helps bats find them in the dark. By morning the blooms are wide open for daytime visitors too.

Bats flutter from flower to flower to sip the sugary nectar. As they feed they carry pollen along with them, which helps the cactus grow fruit and seeds. Bats are some of the saguaro's most helpful little friends.
facts.artAlt: A bat hovers at the creamy white flowers on top of a saguaro cactus at night, its face dusted with pale pollen
facts.caption: A bat sips nectar from a saguaro flower in the dark.

facts.text: A saguaro can grow to about 40 feet tall, higher than a house. It usually does not grow its first arm until it is 50 to 70 years old, and many live for 150 to 175 years. That means some of these giants are older than your great great grandparents.
facts.artAlt: One enormous saguaro cactus with several thick arms towers over the desert scrub, red mesas far behind
facts.caption: One saguaro, standing tall above the desert scrub.

infographic.title: How tall is a saguaro?
infographic.caption: The saguaro's height comes from the National Park Service. The everyday sizes are here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: Ships of the Sandy Sea
pages.artAlt: A line of camels walks across a sandy dune while the sun rises behind them

facts.text: A camel's hump does not hold water like a water bottle. It is actually full of fat, which the camel's body can turn into energy when food is hard to find. A healthy, well fed camel has a nice plump hump.

After a long dry spell a thirsty camel can gulp as much as 38 gallons of water in one drink, which is a whole lot of buckets. It can also travel a week or more without any water at all. That makes the camel a champion at desert life.
facts.artAlt: A camel drinks from a trough of clear water at a desert well, water dripping from its muzzle
facts.caption: A camel takes a long drink at a desert well.

facts.text: Camels are built for blowing sand. They have double rows of long eyelashes, noses they can squeeze shut, and wide padded feet that spread out so they do not sink. All of this helps them stride across the dunes with ease.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a camel's head in profile, its very long double eyelashes and closed slit nostrils clearly visible
facts.caption: Double eyelashes and nostrils that squeeze shut keep the sand out.

infographic.title: How much can a camel drink?

rows.label: A kid's water bottle
rows.display: about a quarter of a gallon

rows.label: A thirsty camel, in one drink

infographic.caption: The camel's big drink comes from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. The bottle, the bucket and the bathtub are everyday sizes, and they show that a thirsty camel can drink almost a whole bathtub in one go.

pages.title: The Little Desert Dragon
pages.artAlt: A small spiky horned lizard rests on cracked orange desert ground

facts.text: Horned lizards love to munch on ants. They use a sticky tongue to snap up big harvester ants one at a time. Because ants are such a tiny snack, these lizards need to eat a great many of them.

A horned lizard's skin can be beige, tan, brown or slightly red to match the desert soil around it. This color trick lets it blend right in with the ground. Sitting still, it can be very tricky to spot.
facts.artAlt: A tan and beige horned lizard sits perfectly still on cracked orange desert soil, almost the same color as the ground
facts.caption: Sitting still on the desert soil, the lizard nearly disappears.

facts.text: The pointy spikes give this lizard its name and help keep it safe. When a hungry animal comes close, the lizard can puff up its wide, flat body to look bigger and harder to gobble up. Snakes find these round, spiky lizards a real mouthful.
facts.artAlt: A close-up of a horned lizard's head showing its crown of pointed horns and the spiky scales along its wide flat body
facts.caption: The crown of spikes that gives the horned lizard its name.

infographic.title: How tiny is a desert dragon?
infographic.caption: The lizard's length comes from the Nevada Department of Wildlife. The everyday sizes are here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: A Green Surprise in the Sand
pages.artAlt: Tall palm trees and a pool of water sit in the middle of golden desert sand

facts.text: An oasis appears where hidden underground water reaches the surface. This often happens along cracks in the rock called fault lines, where hard stone pushes the water up. Suddenly there is a cool, wet spot in the dry desert.
The tall trees at many desert oases are California fan palms. They have huge fan-shaped leaves that can be as long as you are tall. These leafy giants can grow very tall and live for many years.
facts.artAlt: Looking straight up into the crown of a California fan palm, its huge fan-shaped leaves spreading across a blue sky
facts.caption: Looking straight up into the fan-shaped leaves of a desert palm.

facts.text: Animals travel from all around to rest in the cool shade and drink the steady water. Birds such as orioles even build their nests under the palm leaves. An oasis is a busy, happy place in the middle of the sand.
facts.artAlt: Small birds perch and fly in the shade of palm fronds beside a still green oasis pool
facts.caption: Birds gather in the shade beside the oasis pool.

infographic.title: How an oasis appears in the sand

stops.label: Rain soaks into the ground far away and sinks deep underground
The water creeps sideways through the rock, hidden under the desert
Hard rock along a crack pushes it back up, and a pool appears

infographic.caption: It can take a very long time for water to travel underground before it finally reaches the light.
